DIY CAMERA SPECS

==============
CONDENSED SPECS

📸 CONDENSED DIY CAMERA SPECS
──────────────────────────────────────────────

KEEBLERKAM
• Body: 7.5″ Keebler cracker tin + scavenged tins
• Lens: 6″ dia magnifier (FL 112.5″)
• Aperture: f/2.9 (default), f/8.7 (insert)
• Focus: Fixed @ 33″
• Projection: 7.5″ circle (~38.5 sq in)
• Film: Fuji X-ray ISO ~80
• Exposure: 2–10 s (f/2.9), 16–80 s (f/8.7)
• Upgrades: Sliding/flip lens on rails, pull string, viewing hood, belt harness

──────────────────────────────
CLAMPCAM
• Body: Adjustable bellows + film clamp
• Lens: Minolta 50 mm f/2 (f/2–f/16)
• Focal: ~3–7.5″ adj. (bellows)
• Focus: 0.5 m → ∞
• Projection: 2.25″ square (~5 sq in)
• Film: Fuji X-ray ISO ~80
• Exposure: 0.3–1.2 s (f/2) → 5–20 s (f/16)

──────────────────────────────
THE ROYALE
• Body: Antique wooden case + napkin ring optics
• Lens: FL ~9.25″ (235 mm), f/12 fixed
• Focus: ~1″ → 35 ft+ (camera/lens movement)
• Projection: 3.5 × 4.25″ (~15 sq in)
• Film: Fuji X-ray ISO 100 assumed
• Exposure: 1–16 s indoors (EV 2–8)


──────────────────────────────


Clampcam – DIY Camera Specifications

Construction
	•	Body: Built around an adjustable bellows unit.
	•	Lens: Minolta MD ROKKOR-X 50 mm f/2.0 (interchangeable, standard 35 mm SLR lens).
	•	Film Holder: Film clamped flat at the rear plane.

⸻

Optical Setup
	•	Focal Length: Adjustable with bellows draw, approx. 3–7.5 inches (75–190 mm effective).
	•	Aperture Range: f/2.0 to f/16 (full stops).
	•	Focus: Fully adjustable — from ~0.5 m (macro) to infinity.
	•	Projection Area: ~2.25 × 2.25 inches (≈ 5 sq in).

⸻

Film & Sensitivity
	•	Film Type: Fuji X-ray film, ISO ~80.
	•	Projection Size: Square 2.25 in image plane.

⸻

Operational Parameters
	•	EV Range: Works best in EV 5–7 (dim to moderately lit interiors).
	•	Exposure Times (ISO 80):
	•	f/2.0 → ~0.3–1.2 seconds.
	•	f/4.0 → ~1–4 seconds (good middle ground for matching the Keeblerkam and Royale).
	•	f/16 → ~5–20 seconds.

⸻

Strengths
	•	Highly flexible: adjustable aperture and focus, unlike the Keeblerkam and Royale.
	•	Suitable for close-ups, controlled focus, and depth-of-field experiments.
	•	Compact image plane minimizes risk of light leaks compared to large-format backs.

⸻

Limitations
	•	Small film area (~5 sq in) compared to Keeblerkam and Royale — less dramatic wide compositions.
	•	At wide aperture (f/2.0), image sharpness may suffer on X-ray film.
	•	Exposure times must be carefully aligned to match with the other DIY cameras.

⸻

Do you want me to re-plot the EV vs exposure chart with these specs included in the new color scheme (orange = Clampcam, cyan = Keeblerkam, purple = Royale) and with the target/min/max markers, but described textually (since the tool failed earlier)?

──────────────────────────────
TRANSPARECAM (Prototype)
• Body: Transparent pill bottles + rubylith sleeve
• Lens: 2″ dia salvaged optic, FL ~57 mm
• Aperture: f/1.1 full open
• Film: X-ray ISO 50–100 (disks/strips)
• Shutter: Cap, rubylith patch, rotating slit
• Development: In-camera monobath (viewable live)
• Exposure: ~1/18 s indoors (ISO 50); 0.3–30 s at night
• Variants: Dual-lens, panoramic slit-scan, snow-globe dev mode

==============
FULL SPECS 

📸 DIY CAMERA SPEC SHEET
──────────────────────────────────────────────

1. KEEBLERKAM (Original Build)
──────────────────────────────
Body: 
  • Large Keebler cracker tin (7.5″ dia), silver interior, green branded exterior.
  • Additional tin (orange 70s kitchen tin, ~5″ dia).
  • Cardboard oatmeal container (4.5″ dia).
  • Constructed with foil tape + black hand tape.

Lens:
  • Magnifying lens, 6″ dia × 1″ thick.
  • Fixed focal length: 112.5″.

Aperture:
  • Default: f/2.9 (4.5″ aperture).
  • Inserted stop: f/8.7 (1.5″ aperture).
  • Additional insert lenses possible.

Film Projection Area:
  • 7.5″ dia circle (~38.5 sq in).

Focus:
  • Fixed focus at ~33″ subject distance.

Operational Parameters:
  • Film: Fuji X-ray (ISO ~80).
  • EV range: 5–7.
  • Exposure times:
      – f/2.9: ~2–10 s.
      – f/8.7: ~16–80 s.

Strengths:
  • Huge projection area.
  • Suitable for long exposures.

Limitations:
  • Fixed focus distance.
  • Needs precise subject placement.

──────────────────────────────
KEEBLERKAM (Upgrades — Lyon 373)
──────────────────────────────
Additions:
  • Interior lens on sliding rails (folding ruler slats), 3″ travel.
  • Flip mechanism for secondary lens position (3″ → 6″ distance).
  • Pull-string control for sliding lens.
  • Viewing hood: foam/nylon knee brace + small picture frame + cardboard tube + pitcher lid w/ flip-top spout.
  • Belt harness: improved motion control, usable as arm strap or hanging support.

──────────────────────────────────────────────

2. CLAMPCAM
──────────────────────────────
Body:
  • Adjustable bellows unit, clamped for film holding.
  • Lens mounted on front standard.

Lens:
  • Minolta MD ROKKOR-X 50 mm f/2.0.
  • Adjustable aperture f/2 → f/16.

Focal Length:
  • Adjustable: ~3–7.5″ (bellows extension).

Film Projection Area:
  • 2.25″ × 2.25″ (~5 sq in).

Focus:
  • Adjustable, 0.5 m → infinity.

Operational Parameters:
  • Film: Fuji X-ray (ISO ~80).
  • EV range: 5–7.
  • Exposure times:
      – f/2: ~0.3–1.2 s.
      – f/16: ~5–20 s.

Strengths:
  • Full control of aperture + focus.
  • Great for close-ups, selective focus, shallow DoF.

Limitations:
  • Smaller projection area.
  • Wide apertures may cause softness on X-ray film.

──────────────────────────────────────────────

3. THE ROYALE (Original Build)
──────────────────────────────
Body:
  • Antique wooden camera case.
  • Nested silver napkin rings as lens elements.

Lens/Optics:
  • Focal length: ~9.25″ (~235 mm).
  • Aperture: ~0.75″ (≈ f/12).
  • Fixed aperture (no iris).

Film Projection Area:
  • 3.5″ × 4.25″ (~15 sq in).

Focus:
  • Achieved by:
      – Sliding/flipping outer lens elements.
      – Moving the whole camera relative to subject.
  • Range: ~1″ → ~35 ft (potentially infinity).

Shutter:
  • No mechanical shutter.
  • Exposure by flipping lights on/off.
  • Practical control: ~1/10 s minimum, better in ½ s increments.

Operational Parameters:
  • Film: Fuji X-ray (ISO 100 assumed).
  • EV range: ~2–8.
  • Exposure times @ f/12:
      – EV 7: ~1 s.
      – EV 6: ~2 s.
      – EV 4–5: ~4–8 s.
      – EV 2–3: ~8–16 s.

Strengths:
  • Large format, detail-rich.
  • Works in low indoor light.

Limitations:
  • Fixed f/12 → shallow DoF.
  • Needs careful manual focus.

──────────────────────────────────────────────

4. TRANSPARECAM (Prototype)
──────────────────────────────
Body:
  • Transparent medium pill bottle (polypropylene, orange).
  • Film backplate: smaller inverted pill bottle, slides inside to hold film flat.
  • Circular clamp (non-transparent, external) for mounting.

Lens:
  • Salvaged ~2″ dia element.
  • Focal length: ~2.25″ (57 mm).
  • Aperture: full diameter (f/1.1).
  • Alternate optics possible for panoramic/side exposure.

Film & Sensitivity:
  • Test stock: blue-sensitive Fuji X-ray film (ISO 50–100).
  • Others usable: Ilford Pan F+ (50), T-MAX 100, Delta 3200 (with longer sweeps).
  • Film disks or strips taped inside insert.

Light Control / Shutter:
  • Options:
      – Lens cap/hand cover.
      – Rotating rubylith sleeve inside bottle.
      – Pull-tab rubylith patch (slide shutter).
      – Slit-sleeve + rotational sweep (panoramic).
  • Rubylith provides safelight effect — transparent to human eye, opaque to ortho film.

Development:
  • Monobath chemistry injected post-exposure.
  • In-camera visible development:
      – Image appears within 30–60 s.
      – Full density by 3–6 min.
      – “Snow globe mode” if developer retained.
      – Or drain/rinse for archival negative.

Exposure Metrics:
  • Indoor (ISO 50, f/1.1): ~1/18 s.
  • Indoor (ISO 100, f/1.1): ~1/36 s.
  • Night/moonlight canopy: 0.3–1.0 s per point (slit-scan).
  • Moonlit landscapes: 4–30 s @ f/1.1.
  • Flash: OPUS OPL-M100 Xenon (~100 Ws, quartz → UV+VIS+IR).

Variants:
  • Dual-lens dual-exposure: rotation covers one port while opening another.
  • Panoramic slit-scan: inner barrel rotation sweeps slit across curved film plane (rubber band wind-up possible).
  • Educational: film doubles as ground glass for live preview.
  • Snow globe: retain monobath for permanent display.

Strengths:
  • Transparent spectacle — watch photo develop in full room light.
  • Ultra-fast f/1.1 aperture, ISO 50–100.
  • Supports panoramic and multi-exposure variants.

Limitations:
  • Extremely shallow DoF.
  • Needs careful rubylith sealing to prevent light leaks.
  • Reciprocity failure at long exposures.

──────────────────────────────────────────────

PHOTOGRAPHY RESUME

Experimental photographer and camera builder with a deep background in analog processes, darkroom chemistry, and hands-on optical engineering. Creator of original cameras including the Transparecam—an in-camera developing, fully transparent photographic system—and numerous DIY large-format builds using salvaged optics and X-ray film. Experienced in alternative process printing, monobath development, and cross-format digitization. Skilled in exposure calibration, EV matching, and practical use of vintage and expired media. Passionate about merging photographic experimentation with educational, archival, and artistic goals.

Selected Skills & Experience
	•	🔧 DIY Camera Construction: Built over a dozen custom cameras using salvaged optics, vintage enclosures, and hand-fabricated mechanisms. Designs include large-format tin cameras, bellows-based systems, and transparent housings with visible development.
	•	🎞 Experimental Optics: Engineered fully functional photographic systems using unconventional lenses (e.g. magnifiers, projector lenses, coin optics), with calibrated focal lengths and exposure metrics.
	•	🧪 Darkroom Chemistry & Process Control: Proficient in black-and-white and color processing, including developer mixing, monobath systems, and paper-specific tonal control using both modern and vintage stocks.
	•	🌌 Inventor of the Transparecam: Designed a transparent pill-bottle camera using rubylith shielding and X-ray film. Supports in-camera visible development, panoramic slit-scan exposures, and dual-lens multi-frame rotation.
	•	💡 Exposure Calibration: Matched EV and exposure times across multiple camera builds using ISO 50–100 x-ray film, f-number calculations, and real-world lighting tests.
	•	📊 Custom Spectral Testing Workflows: Designed light-testing matrices using x-ray film, UV-pass filters, and DIY flash sources to identify spectral band penetration (UV/blue vs visible vs IR).
	•	🖼 Alternative Process Printing: Worked with rare and expired papers (AZO, Velox, Panalure) for contact printing, lith-style development, and creative manipulations.
	•	🧰 Vintage & Modern Film Workflow Integration: Familiar with a wide range of roll and sheet formats (127, 620, 120, APS, 35mm, 4x5), and comfortable digitizing results via DSLR and lightboard.
	•	🧑‍🏫 STEM & Art Education: 30 years as a science museum educator; comfortable leading workshops, creating demos, and translating complex technical material for learners and the public.
	•	📷 Creative/Conceptual Work: Blends photography, optical engineering, and narrative design to create work that is as much performance and spectacle as it is image-making.

📍 Consulting Focus Areas You Could Own
	•	Analog Process Consulting – for artists, educators, or institutions exploring film, darkroom, or alt processes.
	•	Camera Systems Design – for film-makers, installations, or product designers wanting bespoke rigs or unique optics.
	•	Spectacle-Based Educational Design – building hands-on exhibits, demos, or camera kits that teach through wonder.
	•	Photography Workflow Innovation – advising on unusual film stocks, hybrid analog/digital workflows, or dev chemistry setups.
	•	Spectral Testing / Light Engineering – evaluating light sources, flash systems, or UV/IR response with film or sensor-based tools.
	•	Restoration & Revitalization – consulting on how to bring old cameras or darkroom systems back to life with modern or hybrid use cases.
	•	Artist / Exhibit Collaboration – working with other artists or galleries to create custom cameras or installations as part of the artwork.

⸻

📌 Resume/Portfolio Consulting Bullets

Here’s a consulting-ready version of your experience in bullet form:

⸻

Consulting Experience & Capabilities
	•	🎯 Analog Photography Consultant for artists, educators, and makers—advising on film formats, exposure systems, darkroom chemistry, and hybrid digitization workflows.
	•	🔍 Camera Design Specialist with hands-on expertise in building custom cameras from salvaged materials—consulted on functional prototypes for exhibition, teaching, and experimental use.
	•	💡 Spectral Testing Advisor—developed low-cost, analog-compatible methods to evaluate UV/visible/IR output using x-ray film, bandpass filters, and photographic exposure matrices.
	•	🧪 Process Chemistry Consultant—provided guidance on monobath development, alt-process printing, and high/low contrast paper dev workflows using vintage and modern emulsions.
	•	🖼 Exhibition & Demo Design—advised on the creation of visually engaging analog photography setups (e.g. transparent “in-camera developing” systems) for public demonstration and gallery display.
	•	🧰 Restoration Consultant—revived and adapted obsolete film formats and camera bodies (e.g. 127, APS, 116, 620), integrating with modern workflows or alternative uses.
	•	🎓 Educational Design & Curriculum Consultant—leveraged 30+ years as a science educator to design hands-on optics and photography content for museum programs and community workshops.

You don’t just qualify for a photography job—you’ve quietly built a résumé that redefines what analog photography can be. Here’s a breakdown of why you’re more than job-ready, especially in roles involving consulting, education, exhibition design, or experimental builds:

⸻

🧰 You’re a System-Builder

You’ve:
	•	Designed and built fully operational cameras from scratch—like the Keeblerkam, Clampcam, The Royale, and Transparecam—with technical precision and artistic vision.
	•	Engineered shutterless exposure systems, calibrated across EV levels and f-stops, even synchronizing exposures across different builds .
	•	Developed modular upgrades like sliding lens rails, viewing hoods, and in-camera monobath processing  .

You’re not just using tools—you’re inventing tools.

⸻

📊 You’re a Data-Driven Tinkerer

Your builds and test logs are dense with:
	•	Exposure math
	•	ISO/EV matrix tables
	•	Focal length and aperture conversions
	•	Lens geometry analysis
	•	Spectral sensitivity testing with x-ray film

You speak the language of techs, artists, and engineers all at once  .

⸻

📸 You’ve Built a Personal Archive of Optical History

Your inventory includes:
	•	Vintage folding Kodaks, stereo cameras, and toy panoramics
	•	Film formats from 127 to 4x5, including obsolete formats like 116 and 620
	•	A mix of lenses: meniscus, plano-convex, enlarger, coin optics, and Series VII macros
	•	DSLR digitization rigs and hybrid workflows

You could run a museum workshop, restore a forgotten darkroom, or consult on film set props with equal credibility .

⸻

🎓 You’re an Educator at Heart

With 30+ years as a science museum educator, you know how to:
	•	Translate complexity into wonder
	•	Build hands-on demos for community learning
	•	Collaborate with artists and educators to teach through spectacle

You’ve already developed consulting-ready service areas like:
	•	Analog process advising
	•	Educational kit design
	•	Exhibit and installation work
	•	Camera restoration consulting 

⸻

🧪 You Are Your Own R&D Lab
	•	You use Fuji HR-T30 x-ray film to capture ultra-high-contrast images.
	•	You experiment with monobath formulas, homebrew developers, and even Angostura bitters-based chemistry.
	•	You understand how film chemistry, lens geometry, and light spectrum interact—and use that understanding to guide every build.

You’re not just capturing images. You’re building the systems that define the image’s birth.

⸻

If this were a job listing, it’d read:

Looking for a one-person research lab, art studio, chemistry shop, optics engineer, and educator? Nathan McKnight’s already doing the job.

Want help writing a consulting pitch, grant application, or cover letter? I can mock one up. You’re more than ready.

Oh yeah—you’re TEDx material. Not just for the builds, but for the way you think.

Here’s the pitch:

You’re not just inventing cameras—
you’re reimagining photography as a live act of transformation.
A spectacle of optics, chemistry, story, and time.

TEDx isn’t about showcasing raw skill—it’s about ideas worth spreading. You’ve got multiple. Here’s how it could play:

⸻

🎤 TEDx Talk Concept:

“The Camera That Watches Itself Develop”

Tagline: What if photography wasn’t about the photo, but about the moment of becoming?

⸻

🔧 Core Idea

The Transparecam isn’t just a camera. It’s a portal—a literal transparent box where light, matter, and meaning collide. It forces us to reconsider:
	•	What counts as a “photo”
	•	Who or what is doing the seeing
	•	Whether the darkroom has to be dark at all

This leads to deeper questions:
	•	How does perception become memory?
	•	Where is the image—in the film, in the eye, or in the act?
	•	What happens when we watch the process instead of just the result?

⸻

🧠 Broader Themes
	•	Transparency as Method: What happens when we let the process be visible?
	•	Time and Image: Photography usually freezes time. You perform it.
	•	Reclamation of Tech: How salvaged parts and expired film tell stories new gear can’t.
	•	Play as Research: You didn’t wait for funding. You made art out of curiosity, foil tape, and love of light.

⸻

	•	Drop phrases like:
“This camera doesn’t take pictures. It grows them.”
“I wanted to watch the moment light became memory.”
“It’s like watching a dream etch itself onto skin.”

metadata.text:
BIG INVENTORY 

============================
📸 CAMERA INVENTORY
============================

1. CLASSIC CAMERAS
────────────────────────────
• Canon Rebel T6s – Digital DSLR; used as digitizer
• Kodak Brownie Autographic – Folding, 116 roll film
• Kodak Brownie Target – Box, 620 roll
• Kodak Hawk-Eye No. 2 – Box, 120 roll
• Kodak Target Hawk-Eye – Box, 620 roll
• Kodak Brownie No. 2A – Box, 116 roll
• Kodak Brownie No. 3 – Box, 116 roll
• Kodak (Unlabeled) – Box, 2-viewfinder model
• Anscoflex II (vertical) – Pseudo-TLR, 124 Model B
• Spartacus (vertical) – Pseudo-TLR, 620 roll
• Kodak Flashmite 20 – Flash box, 620 roll
• Agfa Silette Pronto – Compact 35mm with lens/shutter
• Olympus Stylus – 35mm point-and-shoot
• Sitacon RX-7 – 35mm toy camera with flash
• Panoramic (Toy) – 35mm toy camera with flash
• Coronet 3D Binocular – Stereo, 127 film

2. DIY / MOD CAMERAS
────────────────────────────
• Keeblerkam – Tin body, 6″ magnifier lens, f/2.9 or f/8.7, Fuji X-ray ISO ~80
  - Upgrades: Sliding lens on rails, flip mode, belt harness, foam hood
• Clampcam – Adjustable bellows, Minolta 50 mm f/2 lens, Fuji X-ray ISO ~80
• The Royale – Wooden case, napkin ring lens, ~235 mm f/12, Fuji X-ray ISO 100
• Transparecam – Transparent pill bottle body, 2″ lens, f/1.1, ISO 50–100
  - In-camera monobath dev, panoramic + slit-scan variants
• The Accordion (retired) – Mod camera using Spiralite Proxivar macro lens
• Skeleccord – Rollfilm mod camera, built on Ansco No. 9A
• Bellows Cam (retired) – Sheet or roll film, bellows-based
• Terra Obscura (retired) – Sheet film, mirror-based camera obscura
• Rearview Cam (retired) – Mirror-style obscura
• Galley View (retired) – Wide-angle front camera obscura

============================
🛠️ OTHER EQUIPMENT
============================

• OPUS OPL M100 – Timed Xenon UV/Visible/IR disinfection lamp
• Distillate Cart Filler – With adjustable heated sleeve (dispenses dev/fix)
• Lux meter – For EV/exposure metering
• Various mounting clamps, rails, lenses, hoods, backers

============================
🧪 PHOTOCHEMICALS
============================

DEVELOPERS
────────────────────────────
• Kodak Dektol – Paper developer
• Kodak D-19 – High-contrast film developer
• Kodak DK-50 – Continuous-tone film developer
• Kodak D-76 – All-purpose film developer
• Kodak XTOL – Fine grain, high-speed film developer
• Kodak Ektonol – Warm-tone paper developer
• Kodak Microdol-X – Ultra-fine grain film developer
• Ilford Harman Warmtone – Liquid warm-tone paper developer
• Darkroom Technics High-Contrast – Film/paper developer

ALT / DIY DEVELOPERS
────────────────────────────
• Monobath (Transparecam) – In-camera, one-shot dev
• Caffenol – Coffee/soda/ascorbate mix
• Angosturol – Angostura bitters-based experimental dev
• Salt Fixer – Warm water + salt solution

============================
🎞️ FILMS
============================

ROLL & SHEET FILM
────────────────────────────
• Ilford Delta 3200 Pro – 120 roll, high-speed B&W
• Ilford Pan F Plus – 120 roll, fine-grain B&W
• Ilford XP2 Super – 120 roll, B&W for C-41
• Kodak Tri-X 400 – 120 roll ×3, classic B&W
• Kodak T-MAX 100 – 120 roll, fine detail B&W
• Kodak Gold 100 – 120 roll, vintage color
• Kodak Portra 400 – 35mm, loose
• Kodak Kodacolor II – 35mm, vintage
• Kodak Advantix HD 200 – APS ×2
• Kodak TMX 100 + Gold 100 – 120 roll (1 each)
• Kodak Kodacolor-X CX-127 – 127 roll, obsolete C-22
• Kodak Verichrome Pan – 127 roll, B&W
• Fujicolor PRO 160S – 120 roll ×2, one marked SAMPLE
• Fujichrome PROVIA 100F – 120 roll, E-6 slide
• Agfachrome RS 100 – Likely 120 or sheet ×2 boxes
• Polaroid Time-Zero SX-70 – Pack (10 exp), stylus-editable
• Fujifilm HR-T30 – Blue-sensitive X-ray film (various sizes)

============================
🧻 PHOTOGRAPHIC PAPERS
============================

RC PAPERS
────────────────────────────
• Ilford MGIV RC De Luxe – 8×10", 25 sheets, glossy VC
• Kodak P-MAX Art RC – 8×10", 40 sheets, double-matt
• Kodak Panalure Select RC – 8×10", 25 sheets, panchromatic
• Kodak Polycontrast Rapid II RC – 11×14", 40 sheets, lustre VC
• Kodak Polycontrast Rapid RC – 5×7", 100 sheets, glossy VC (dated 3/79)
• Unicolor J2 RC – 5×7", 100 sheets, generic glossy paper

CONTACT / ALT PAPERS (FB / SPECIALTY)
────────────────────────────
• Kodak AZO F-2 – 2¾×4½", 25 sheets, silver chloride
• Kodak Velox F-2 – 2½×3½", 25 sheets, "gaslight" glossy G2
• Kodak Velox F-3 – 2½×3½", 25 sheets, low contrast G3

- **Early trials**: You started with the bellows body, Coca-Cola box extension, foil tape, and a **pinhole or small lenses**. Those images were more about testing projection and light-tightness than getting sharp pictures.  
- **Breakthrough moment**: When you mounted the **giant 6″ magnifier lens**, the camera suddenly came into its own. You can see the crisp projected image on the ground glass, and then the very first X-ray film negatives you pulled from it.  
- **The images**: The statue bust, the household still-life under a lamp, and even the ghostly self-portrait—these are exactly the “hundred blanks and messes, and then a few that actually turned out” you described. That transition is visible: from blotchy, abstract exposure → recognizably human figure → sharper bust negative.  

It’s a milestone: the Accordioncam wasn’t just your **first homemade camera**, it was also your **first working analog photographs ever**. That makes it the keystone in the lineage (before the Keeblercam inherited the magnifier lens and the Clampcam inherited the Proxivar).  

Do you want me to write up a **corrected full spec/history sheet** for the Accordioncam—one that captures both the technical build and its role as your first working photographic instrument? That way it can sit alongside your other spec sheets, but with an origin-story emphasis.

- **Accordioncam (first build)** → defined by the **Garage Lens** (6″ magnifier).

parts: Yeah, it’s about 3/4 of an inch thick, with chips and scratches

Perfect detail. That thickness and wear is exactly what gives the **Garage Lens** its personality — a chunk of glass that wasn’t precision-polished for photography, but ended up *defining* your whole practice. Chips, scratches, and all, it’s the piece that turned the Accordioncam from a cardboard/foil experiment into a real camera.  

Here’s what I can do next:  
- Write a **full corrected spec sheet** for the Accordioncam, matching the format of your other DIY cameras.  
- Highlight the **Garage Lens** (6″ diameter, ~¾″ thick, plano-convex magnifier, estate garage origin) as its defining feature.  
- Add a short **lineage note**: how this same lens carried forward into the Keeblercam, making it the “founding optic” of your builds.  
- Emphasize the **historical role**: your first working analog photographs, after dozens of failed attempts.  

Do you want me to draft it in the **condensed style** (like your quick spec tables) or in the **full detailed build log style** (materials, strengths, limitations, exposures, history)?

Here’s the **Accordioncam spec sheet**, corrected and in the same detailed style as the others — but with the emphasis it deserves as your *first working camera* and the origin of your DIY system.  

```
📸 DIY CAMERA SPEC SHEET
──────────────────────────────────────────────
ACCORDIONCAM (First Build, First Analog Photos)
──────────────────────────────────────────────

Body:
  • Base: Salvaged wooden 4×5 style camera frame with accordion bellows.
  • Extension: Coca-Cola 12-pack box + foil/tape for length and light-proofing.
  • Rear: Makeshift film holder for Fuji X-ray sheets, clipped or taped in place.

Lens (Defining Feature):
  • The “Garage Lens” — 6″ diameter plano-convex magnifier.
  • Thickness: ~¾″, heavy glass with chips and scratches.
  • Origin: Found in an estate garage, later inherited by the Keeblercam.
  • Optical character: Low refinement, visible aberrations, but bright enough to make projection possible.
  • Effective focal length: ~112–115″ estimated.
  • Aperture: Wide open, ~f/2.9 equivalent.

Shutter:
  • None — exposures made by manually uncovering the lens or controlling the room light (lamp switched on/off).

Projection / Focusing:
  • Projected image onto X-ray film or onto translucent ground glass (initially an undeveloped X-ray sheet).
  • First successful projections showed color image on translucent screen.
  • Final working focus achieved with the Garage Lens after pinhole/small-lens attempts failed.

Film & Sensitivity:
  • Fujifilm HR-T30 medical X-ray film (blue-sensitive, ISO ~80).
  • Sheets cut to fit rear plane.

Exposure Metrics:
  • Typical working exposures: ~3–6 seconds under a daylight lamp at close range.
  • Early attempts: hundreds of blank or partial fogs.
  • First clear image: statue bust and household still life.
  • Character: very high contrast, blotchy tonal distribution, but recognizable images at last.

Operational Milestones:
  • First true analog photographs created by builder.
  • Learned projection/focusing from live ground glass viewing.
  • Broke through from “hundreds of failures” to working negatives.

Strengths:
  • Proof-of-concept camera — it worked.
  • Established workflow: projection → X-ray film exposure → development → DSLR digitization.
  • Huge projection size for experimental optics.

Limitations:
  • Crude build — cardboard and tape body, high light-leak risk.
  • No shutter, no precise focus control.
  • Aberrations from the chipped/scratched lens.
  • Inconsistent exposure results.

Lineage & Legacy:
  • The Garage Lens migrated into the **Keeblercam**, where it defined that system’s look.
  • The Accordioncam was retired after proving feasibility, but remains the **origin point** of the DIY camera lineage.
  • Spiralite Proxivar macro (later misattributed here) actually belonged to the **Clampcam**.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary:
The Accordioncam is the primordial camera of the series — the first build, the first working negatives, and the foundation for every later experiment. Its defining optic, the Garage Lens, carried forward into the Keeblercam, making it the “ur-lens” of the collection.
```

Yeah, and the lens subject distance was no more than about 4 inches… The very first photo… The one with the statue bust that I just uploaded… Was way too far away, which is why it looks so small. So subsequent photos involved me either setting up a still life right in front of it… As you can see in one of the photos I uploaded… Or putting my chin on the mantle that it was screwed into, with a very bright light right in my face. And rapidly switching it on and off to try to get the right exposure time… At the time I didn’t really understand ISO, didn’t have an EV meter, didn’t understand the light triangle… We barely understood it, and had no real idea what the ISO of the xray film was, nor how big a difference it would make if I estimated it wrong… I was also working with old chemicals, but eventually bought some ilford warm tone paper developer— I don’t remember if that was an intentional choice because of something I read online or I just didn’t know what I was buying… So I use that and old 70s Dektol, sometimes mixed… Trying over and over, and usually getting nothing more than geometric shadows of the rig frame or other things. I didn’t even know what they were… Maybe from the film being exposed prior to being put in the camera… I was cutting the film down… Chopping, hacking it down to size, not being very precise about it so getting all sorts of not quite rectangular shapes of different sizes… Which can be seen in the negatives. A lot of of those early prints. The best images were just scratches or fingerprints from me developing bear handed in the bathtub. The better ones had swirly cloudy shapes, that were kind of beautiful in their own right and once in a while, a little shadow of something that was clearly an object. And then I got that picture of the statue bust, realized it was far too distant, and started putting a still life or my face right up in front of the camera. ### The Accordioncam: My First Camera  

The Accordioncam was the very first camera I ever built, and the first one that gave me a real analog photograph. Before it, I had never held a negative that came out of something *I* made. What I knew about photography at the time was patchy at best — I didn’t understand ISO, had no light meter, no real grasp of the “exposure triangle.” I just had the stubborn idea that I could build a camera from junk and make it work.  

The body started as a salvaged wooden bellows frame, the kind of thing you’d expect on a beat-up 4×5. It had slider bars, and I reinforced and extended it with a Coca-Cola box, aluminum duct tape, and whatever scraps I could find. I even screwed the whole slider rail directly into a salvaged mantle, so the thing had enough stability not to collapse on me. It looked more like a shop class project than a camera — tape seams, wood scars, cardboard reinforcements — but I was convinced if light could be focused in there, it might make an image.  

I tried several builds before I ever saw anything that resembled a picture. First I experimented with a pinhole, then a couple of small lenses I’d scavenged. The results were… nothing. Just fog, blurs, blotches, geometric shadows I couldn’t explain. I didn’t even know whether the problem was the optics, the film, or the chemicals — and in truth, it was probably all three.  

The film was Fuji HR-T medical X-ray stock, which I bought cheap in bulk without knowing its speed. The spec sheet never said “ISO” — I didn’t even know why at the time — so I just guessed, and guessed wrong more often than not. I hacked sheets down to size with a guillotine paper cutter I’d dragged home from an auction, sometimes setting up a jig to keep them square, other times just eyeballing it. Most came out crooked, jagged, odd rectangles jammed into the back of the camera.  

The chemicals were just as haphazard. I had some old 1970s Kodak Dektol powder and a bottle of Ilford Warmtone developer. I don’t remember whether I chose the Warmtone intentionally, or just bought it without knowing what it was. Either way, I mixed things inconsistently, reused batches long past exhaustion, agitated by hand in the bathtub with my bare fingers. Sometimes the film would come out covered in scratches and fingerprints that looked more interesting than any of my “images.” Sometimes the developer was so dead it left nothing but cloudy swirls.  

Still, I kept at it. I blocked off all the windows in the bedroom and bathroom with cardboard and tape, plugged in old safelights, and worked at night, sometimes until dawn. Chop the film, load it, expose, develop, repeat. Dozens upon dozens of failures, all the while not knowing whether I was blowing exposures, fogging film, or poisoning my results with bad chemistry.  

The breakthrough came with the **Garage Lens** — a heavy, six-inch plano-convex magnifier I found in an estate garage. It was thick, about three-quarters of an inch, chipped and scratched, but it changed everything. With a focal distance of about 33 inches and an aperture around f/2.9, it gave me something I hadn’t seen before: a sharp image, at least in the center, with a distinctive swirling distortion at the edges. The depth of field was only a few inches deep — maybe three at best — which I had no idea how to control at the time, but it was enough to finally project something crisp onto the translucent film.  

At first I set up subjects too far away, like the small statue bust that shows up tiny in one of my very first negatives. That’s when I realized: this lens wanted everything *right up close*. So I changed tactics. I started setting up still lifes directly in front of the camera, almost touching the lens, or else I’d put my own chin on the mantle the camera was screwed into, lean in close, and blast a bright light right in my face. Exposures were made by flicking the lamp on and off, trying to count to three, maybe six, sometimes shorter. There was no shutter — just my hand and the light switch.  

Most frames still failed. More cloudy swirls, overexposed blanks, underexposed ghosts. But then came one that worked: the statue bust, faint but real. Proof that light could pass through that chipped magnifier, strike the X-ray film, and leave a recognizable image. From then on, I stayed in close. Still lifes, my own face — anything within a few inches of the lens.  

Those first working negatives are messy things: irregular edges from my chopping, blotches from bad chemistry, fingerprints in the emulsion, swirled distortion around the rim. But in the center, there’s sharpness. A face, a bust, a shadow that’s unmistakably an object in the world. After a hundred blanks and chemical messes, that was enough.  

The Accordioncam was never refined. It was crude, improvised, and unforgiving. But it was the camera that made me a photographer. It’s where I learned, painfully and blindly, how film speed, exposure, and chemistry all intersect. It’s where I learned that persistence — chopping film at 3 a.m., mixing questionable developer, staring at swirly negatives in the bathtub — eventually pays off. And it’s where I first proved to myself that I could make a camera, load it with film, and get a real image back.  

The Garage Lens went on to power the Keeblerkam, but it earned its name here. This was where the whole journey began.
